topic: Leak analysis: LeakCanary, heap dumps & common leaks

questions.question: How does LeakCanary decide that a destroyed Activity may have leaked?
options: It counts Activity instances in `onCreate` and flags more than one
It asks ActivityManager for activities that were never finished
It watches the destroyed Activity with a weak reference and checks it is still reachable after a delay and a GC
It scans the source for static fields of type Context at build time
questions.explanation: LeakCanary hooks lifecycle callbacks and watches objects that should soon be garbage (destroyed activities, fragment views, cleared ViewModels) via weak references. If one is still there after waiting and running GC, it is retained and LeakCanary dumps the heap to explain why. It does no static analysis.

questions.question: A Kotlin `object` that keeps a reference to an Activity passed to it will leak that Activity after it is destroyed, until the reference is cleared.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: An `object` is a singleton held by a static field, which is a GC root, so anything it references stays reachable. Singletons should hold the application context or nothing context-related at all.

questions.question: LeakCanary reports a leak through `binding` in this Fragment after navigating forward. What is the fix?
options: Make `binding` a `lateinit var` instead of nullable
Set `binding = null` in `onDestroyView()`
Inflate the binding in `onCreate()` instead
Set `binding = null` in `onDestroy()`
questions.explanation: A Fragment on the back stack outlives its view: `onDestroyView()` runs but the Fragment instance stays, so the binding keeps the old view tree alive. Clearing it in `onDestroyView()` fixes that; `onDestroy()` is too late and `lateinit` cannot be cleared at all.

questions.question: Why can an inner `Handler` subclass in an Activity that calls `postDelayed(runnable, 60_000)` leak the Activity?
options: `postDelayed` registers the Activity as a system broadcast receiver
Handlers create a new thread that holds the Activity
The Looper copies the Activity into the MessageQueue for later delivery
The pending Message references the Handler and Runnable, which implicitly reference the Activity, and the main Looper's queue keeps the Message reachable
questions.explanation: The queued Message points to its target Handler and callback; an inner class or capturing lambda holds the outer Activity. The main thread's MessageQueue is reachable from a root, so the Activity stays alive until the message runs. Remove callbacks in the matching lifecycle method or use lifecycle-scoped coroutines.

questions.question: When reading a LeakCanary leak trace, where should you look first for the bad reference?
options: At the leaking object at the bottom, since its own fields hold it
At the references LeakCanary marks as suspect, between the last 'not leaking' node and the first 'leaking' one
At whichever node has the largest retained size
At the GC root at the top, since roots cause every leak
questions.explanation: The trace is the shortest strong reference path from a GC root to the retained object, and LeakCanary labels nodes as leaking or not leaking. The bug is in a reference in the window where the chain goes from 'should be alive' to 'should be gone', which LeakCanary underlines. Roots are often legitimate (like a static singleton) and the leaking object's own fields do not keep it alive.

questions.question: Which of these are likely to leak an Activity? Select all that apply.
options: Launching a long-running coroutine in `GlobalScope` that captures the Activity
Saving the Activity in a companion object field for easy access
Passing the Activity into a function that uses it and returns immediately
Registering an Activity as a listener on a singleton and never unregistering it
Showing a Toast with `applicationContext`
questions.explanation: Singletons, `GlobalScope` jobs and companion object fields all outlive the Activity and keep it reachable. Using the application context does not hold an Activity at all, and a synchronous call that does not store its argument leaves no reference behind.

questions.question: Observing a flow or LiveData in `onViewCreated` with `viewLifecycleOwner` instead of the Fragment itself avoids keeping old views alive and avoids duplicate observers after returning from the back stack.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: The Fragment's own lifecycle continues while it sits on the back stack, so observers tied to it keep referencing the destroyed view and pile up each time a new view is created. The view lifecycle ends at `onDestroyView()`, which removes the observer at the right time.

questions.question: In a heap dump, an object has a shallow size of 32 bytes but a retained size of 40 MB. What does that mean?
options: It has been allocated 40 MB worth of times
40 MB of other objects reference it
The heap dump is corrupt, because retained size cannot exceed shallow size
40 MB of objects are reachable only through it, so freeing it would free all of that
questions.explanation: Retained size is the memory that would be freed if the object were collected: everything it dominates in the reference graph. A tiny object such as a static map or a leaked listener can retain a huge graph. Incoming references do not count toward its retained size.

questions.question: LeakCanary shows this trace. Which changes fix the leak? Select all that apply.
questions.code:
GC Root: static EventBus.listeners
  ↓ ArrayList.elementData
  ↓ MainActivity$onCreate$1 (lambda)
  ↓ MainActivity  (destroyed, LEAKING)
options: Unregister the listener in the lifecycle callback that matches where it was registered
Register through a lifecycle-aware wrapper that removes the listener when the owner is destroyed
Replace the lambda with an anonymous `object :` listener
Change MainActivity's launch mode to `singleTask`
Call `System.gc()` in `onDestroy()`
questions.explanation: The static list keeps the lambda, which captures MainActivity, so the listener must be removed when the Activity goes away, either manually or through lifecycle-aware registration. An anonymous object still captures the Activity, GC cannot free a reachable object, and launch mode does not change the reference chain.

questions.question: Your team wants to run full LeakCanary-style heap dumps on every user's device in production. What is the main problem?
options: Heap dumps exclude Kotlin objects, so they are useless for Kotlin apps
Dumping the heap freezes the app for seconds and the file can be huge and contain user data
Heap dumps can only be taken on rooted devices
LeakCanary cannot detect leaks in release builds because R8 removes all weak references
questions.explanation: Taking an hprof suspends the app while the whole heap is written out, and the dump contains every string in memory, including personal data. That is why it is a debug-build tool, with production approaches relying on sampling, opt-in, or lighter signals. Dumps work without root and include Kotlin objects like any other.
